scenes.text: The chip that started the computer age was built for a desk calculator.
On November fifteenth, nineteen seventy one, Intel put the four zero zero four on sale.
It was the first commercial microprocessor.
A Japanese company called Busicom wanted chips for its new printing calculator.
Their plan needed twelve separate chips.
Intel engineers Ted Hoff and Stan Mazor squeezed the design into just four.
Federico Faggin and Busicom's Masatoshi Shima then designed the processor itself.
Faggin even hid his initials, F F, in a corner of every chip.
The four zero zero four had about two thousand three hundred transistors.
It ran at seven hundred forty kilohertz and handled data just four bits at a time.
Even so, it could add two eight digit numbers in less than a thousandth of a second.
Today's processors run at billions of cycles per second.
And they pack billions of transistors.
Every phone and laptop traces back to that little chip.
What's the oldest gadget you still use?

title: The first microprocessor was made for a calculator 🧮
caption: Intel's 4004 went on sale on Nov 15, 1971, built for a Busicom calculator. 2,300 transistors, 740 kHz, and it changed everything.
